turns: By what substance is heredity passed on from parent to child?
answers: Heredity is passed on from parent to child by means of germs, which are minute particles of living matter, conveyed from the blood of the one to the blood of the other. These germs are so small, that from 30,000 to 40,000 of them may lie side by side in the space of a single linear inch. The germ theory of disease was first clearly established in 1859, by the researches of Louis Pasteur, a French chemist and biologist, who showed that certain maladies were due to the presence of living organisms, which propagated themselves in the affected animal, and produced the specific symptoms of the disorder. The researches of subsequent investigators have extended the scope of the theory, until, at the present time, it may be said to embrace nearly all infective diseases. Germs have been discovered in connexion with smallpox, measles, scarlet fever, typhoid fever, and cholera; in fact, all communicable maladies are now believed to be due to specific causes of this kind. Germs are found not only in the blood, but in the solid tissues of affected animals; and by cultivating them artificially out of the body, in suitable fluids, they may be made to pass, generation after generation, through an almost infinite series. The vitality of germs may be destroyed by exposure to a heat of 140° Fahr., and most of them are killed by drying. Germs are not only the cause of disease, but they are the cause of death; for, when present in sufficient numbers, they prevent the due aëration of the blood, and so arrest the vital functions. In healthy human blood, the proportion of germs is extremely small, but it rises in disease. The practical application of the germ theory has led to important results in sanitary science. It has shown the necessity of purity in air, water, and food, and has made clear the causes of epidemic visitation. The germs of fever are destroyed by disinfectants, and the spread of contagion is checked. The natural history of disease has been studied by means of the microscope, and a school of pathological research has been founded, which already yields fruit of the highest promise.

turns: How does a calculating machine work?
answers: A calculating machine works in precisely the same manner as ordinary arithmetical computation is performed by the mind. Its action consists in arranging digits in certain orders, and then reading off the result. The digits are arranged in lines, each line containing as many figures as there are units in the order of the calculation. The machine is started at the unit place, and works upwards to the left in decimal progression to any required amount. Having arrived at the desired figure, the reader off stops the machine, and announces the total. To prove the accuracy of the work, the process is repeated in a reverse direction, from the highest place downward to the unit. The reading off must, of course, be correct, if the original arrangement of the digits was so. The invention of Mr. Thomas of Colmar, in Alsace, first made public in 1843, was the earliest example of a successful calculating machine; and it still remains unrivalled, both for speed and accuracy. More recently, machines have been produced in England, France, and America, which, though inferior in these qualities, nevertheless perform their tasks with sufficient precision for practical purposes. The great advantage of mechanical computation over mental arithmetic is speed; and in this respect the calculating engines are invaluable to men of business. But they cannot replace the exercise of thought, or spare the necessity of personal supervision. Calculation must still be checked by the intelligence, if not originated by it.

turns: How does a calculating machine work?
answers: A calculating machine works in precisely the same manner as ordinary arithmetical computation is performed by the aid of human agency. The digits to be added, multiplied, or divided, are set down on the machine, in the same way as they are written on paper; and the result is exhibited in a visible form. The invention of Mr. Thomas, of Colmore Row, Birmingham, is so constructed, that, by means of it, addition can be performed with great rapidity and unerring accuracy, from one unit to any number of millions. In multiplication, the machine exhibits the product of two factors, as quickly as the factors can be set down. In division, it shows the quotient, as soon as the dividend and divisor are prepared. And, in extracting the roots of numbers, it displays the result with equal celerity. The principle of the machine may be briefly explained. A series of sliding frames, or boxes, containing digits, from 1 to 9, inclusive, are set in order, at the commencement of an operation; and, as each frame is moved onward, a new digital place is opened. The first, or units place, exhibits 1; the second, 10; the third, 100; and so on, in a tenfold progression, to the last, or ninth place, which shows 900. Should it be desired to accumulate 476, the units digits are set down in the first frame, and the tens in the second; and, by pushing home both frames together, the required sum appears at the tenth, or hundreds place. To multiply 476 by 6, the frames are parted; and, on again closing them, the product, 2856, is disclosed. Division is performed, by leaving the multiplier out of the question, and working with the multiplicand and quotient alone. Lastly, by omitting the dividend and divisor, the machine displays the square root of the quotient. The whole process is so simple and easy of comprehension, that any person may learn to use the invention, in half an hour. The machine occupies little more space than a sheet of foolscap paper; it is portable, and not liable to derangement. The price varies from £15 to £30, according to the number of digital places which it contains.

When a key is touched, a small slide is pushed forward, and a certain number is marked on an arrangement of dials. When the depression of a key has been continued as long as required, the slide returns to its place, and the sum of all the numbers which have been marked on the dials is exhibited in view. The instrument can be made to register any number of figures, from one to nine consecutively, and then to repeat, and so on, ad _infinitum_; and, by an easy contrivance, it can be made to print the numbers which it has indicated. The chief practical use of the machine is, to facilitate and check operations in addition and multiplication of money. In books kept by bankers and merchants, the total of each page is first set down by the machine, and then carried forward to the next. In like manner, the results of long columns of figures are obtained with great expedition, and absolute correctness. The invention of Mr. Charles Babbage, was first publicly exhibited in 1822, and has since undergone various improvements, at the expense of the government. It is still, however, incomplete; but enough has been done to prove its great utility, and to encourage the hope, that, at no distant period, it may be rendered practically serviceable to the purposes of ordinary life.

It was supported by the fact that the specific heat of helium is greater than that of hydrogen, which would be expected if the particles had a greater average distance to move in passing from a lower to a higher temperature. On the other hand, it was pointed out that the atom of helium exhibits greater stability than the atom of hydrogen, and that stability is associated with a packing of the particles in a more close and compact form. The balance of evidence thus appears to be in favour of the view that the atoms of helium and hydrogen are built up on similar plans, but that in helium the plan is executed in more solid fashion than in hydrogen.

turns: The year is 1930. The helium nucleus has a mass of four units but a charge of only two. How do physicists account for this difference?
answers: The nucleus of helium is bivalent, and consequently has a charge of two positive units; but it has also a positive mass of four units, so that the positive charge exactly balances the positive mass. The negative charge is therefore zero, and the nucleus is neutral. On the other hand, the nucleus of hydrogen is univalent, and has a charge of one unit, but a positive mass of only one unit; so that the positive charge exceeds the positive mass by one unit, and the nucleus is consequently ionised. turns: What is an atom made of?
answers: An atom is composed of particles, which are indivisible, and therefore elementary. It is not possible to break up an atom into smaller parts. The atoms of which all matter is composed are similar to one another, and are all of the same weight. The weight of an atom of hydrogen is taken as the unit, and is called a grain. The atom of oxygen weighs sixteen grains, that of sulphur thirty-two grains, and that of carbon six grains. The atoms of all the known elements have now been weighed, and their relative weights are established. The atoms of the same element are all exactly alike in weight, but the atoms of different elements differ from one another in weight. (See CHEMISTRY.)

turns: What is an atom made of?

The molecules of the same element are all precisely similar to each other, and to those of any other element. The molecules of a compound body differ from those of a simple body, in so far as the former are made up of the latter. (See Chemistry.)

The atoms of Democritus were definite in shape, as well as in magnitude; those of Clarke were shapeless. The former were regarded as endowed with active powers of motion, the latter were considered as purely passive. turns: How old is the Earth?
answers: The Earth is supposed to be about 10,000 years old. Geology proves that it has existed for at least that period. The exact age cannot be determined, because the science of geology is yet in its infancy. Palæontology, or the science of fossils, has made great progress, and enables us to speak with tolerable certainty as to the lapse of time since the earliest animals and plants appeared upon the globe. Fossil remains have been discovered, in strata of unquestioned antiquity, of creatures so low in the scale of organisation, that a million of years may have elapsed since the first of them was created. On the other hand, the newest strata contain the relics of animals and vegetables, little, if at all, inferior to those now living upon the earth. Between these two extremes, all grades of organisation are represented. In the present state of geological knowledge, it would be hazardous to affirm, that more than ten millions of years have passed away, since the first living beings were called into existence; but, on the other hand, it would be equally hazardous to assume a shorter period. The Earth may have been created 5,000 years ago, or 50,000,000. Geology can tell us nothing more definite than this.
